issues.claim: the test has three limbs, none of which may be met: no singling out of a record, no linking of records about the same person, and no inference of an attribute
issues.source_says: The guidelines set three criteria, No Record Isolation, No Linkage and No Inference, and state 'If all three criteria are passed ... then the given data can be safely considered anonymous'; 'If any criterion fails, further analysis should be done'. The limbs as the takeaway words them are conditions that must all hold, so 'none of which may be met' inverts the logic.

proposed_takeaway: Data is anonymous only when it no longer relates to an identified or identifiable person for the entity holding it, judged by content, purpose and effect; the test has three limbs, all of which must hold: no singling out of a record, no linking of records about the same person, and no inference of an attribute. The guidelines, which fold in the Court of Justice's September 2025 ruling in EDPS v SRB, allow a contextual assessment (what the actual recipients and reasonably likely third parties can do) or a simplified one applied uniformly. Consultation runs to 30 October 2026; treat every 'anonymised' export, training set or statistic against the three limbs now, and keep the assessment on file, since this is the standard supervisory authorities will apply once the text is final.
note: Relative test, content/purpose/effect, the two assessment approaches, C-413/23 P EDPS v SRB and the 30 October 2026 deadline all confirmed; PDF cover says adopted 7 July 2026 against the site's 08 July 2026 date field.

issues.claim: Article 89(1) safeguards (anonymise or pseudonymise where the purpose allows, ethics review, secure environments, DPIA)
issues.source_says: The safeguards listed in the executive summary are anonymised or pseudonymised data, independent or ethical oversight, secure processing environments, privacy enhancing technologies, protective measures for publication, confidentiality arrangements and conditions for further use. The DPIA appears as a place to document the choice of consent type, not as an Article 89(1) safeguard.

proposed_takeaway: Six indicators decide whether an activity is scientific research (methodical approach, ethical standards, verifiability, independence, societal objective, scientific merit); commercial research qualifies if it is genuinely scientific. The main Article 6 bases are consent, legal obligation, public interest and legitimate interests, with broad consent allowed for defined research areas under extra safeguards, public interest where law provides for it, and legitimate interests weighted in research's favour; special categories need an Article 9(2) condition such as (j) with a legal basis in Union or national law. Further processing for research is presumed compatible under Article 5(1)(b) but still needs its own lawful basis, storage may be extended only for identified projects or a defined research area, and Article 89(1) safeguards (anonymise or pseudonymise where the purpose allows, ethics review, secure environments, privacy enhancing technologies) condition the derogations from erasure, objection and information duties. Adopted 15 April 2026 for consultation to 25 June 2026.
note: Six indicators, commercial research, broad consent, Art. 9(2)(j), Art. 5(1)(b) presumption plus separate basis, extended storage only for specified purposes, 15 April 2026 and 25 June 2026 all confirmed.

proposed_takeaway: Binding implementing act adopted 7 March 2025 under Article 68(1) and in force since 30 March 2025, laying down rules for the establishment and functioning of the scientific panel: selection of experts through an open call, declarations of commitment and confidentiality covering independence and conflicts of interest, the 24-month renewable term, a chair and vice-chair nominated by the members and selected by the Commission, working arrangements with the AI Office and the procedure for qualified alerts to the AI Office under Article 90 when a GPAI model presents a concrete identifiable Union-level risk or should be classified as posing systemic risk. proposed_takeaway: Joint opinion on COM(2025) 836 adopted 20 January 2026. The Board and Supervisor accepted the objective of simplification but asked that any processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection be bound by strict necessity rather than mere necessity and by appropriate safeguards complementing the GDPR, the EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive, that its extension beyond high-risk systems be clearly circumscribed and limited to cases where the risk of adverse effects from bias is sufficiently serious, that data protection authorities stay competent to supervise processing under the new Article 4a and that the AI Office coordinate closely with them where it supervises systems built on general-purpose AI models, and that the obligation to register exempted Annex III systems in the EU database be kept. Non-binding, but it signals how DPAs will read Article 4a.

proposed_takeaway: A 102-page expert report published April 2025 that the EDPB states is not a formal Board position. It maps privacy risks across the eight lifecycle phases of ISO/IEC 22989 and 5338 and across three service models (LLM as a service, off-the-shelf, self-developed), each with its own data flow, sets a three-stage risk methodology of identification, estimation and control, and catalogues technical and organisational mitigations split by provider and deployer role, with three worked use cases. It maps to GDPR Articles 25, 32 and 35 and to the AI Act's provider and deployer roles. Use it as a practical companion to Article 9 risk management and DPIAs for LLM deployments.

issues.source_says: The 2018 document itself says nothing about its successor; it carries only 'Adopted on 3 October 2017, As last Revised and Adopted on 6 February 2018'. The successor claim is accurate but external to this document.

note: wp250rev.01 read in full; CIA breach types, 'not all security incidents are necessarily personal data breaches', 'reasonable degree of certainty', Art 33(1) 72 hours unless unlikely to result in a risk, notification in phases, processor without undue delay and Art 33(5) documentation of all breaches all confirmed.

wp242rev.01, adopted 13 December 2016, last revised 5 April 2017; Art 20(1) format wording, Art 20(2) 'where technically feasible', consent or contract only, 'carried out by automated means', provided plus observed but not inferred or derived, no automatic erasure, Art 12 no fee, 'without hindrance' all confirmed.

wp243rev.01, adopted 13 December 2016, last revised 5 April 2017; Art 37(1)(a) to (c) triggers with the courts-acting-judicially carve-out in footnote 6, Art 37(5) expert knowledge, Art 38(3) no instructions and no dismissal or penalty and direct report to highest management, Art 38(6) conflict of interests over purposes and means, voluntary DPO bound by Arts 37 to 39, Art 37(2) group DPO 'easily accessible from each establishment' all confirmed.

wp251rev.01, adopted 3 October 2017, last revised 6 February 2018; 'Article 22(1) establishes a general prohibition', the three Art 22(2) exceptions, human oversight 'meaningful, rather than just a token gesture', Art 22(3) safeguards attaching to 22(2)(a) and (c) with 22(2)(b) requiring the law itself to lay down suitable measures, 'simple ways to tell the data subject about the rationale behind, or the criteria relied on', and the DPIA point all confirmed.

issues.claim: EDPB Guidelines 8/2022, version 2.0 adopted 28 March 2023, replaced them.
issues.source_says: The 2016/2017 document closes with 'Done in Brussels, on 13 December 2016 ... As last revised and adopted on 05 April 2017' and says nothing about a successor. The successor claim is accurate but external to this document.

note: wp244rev.01 read in full; Art 4(16) main establishment as place of central administration unless decisions taken and implemented elsewhere, 'The GDPR does not permit forum shopping', supervisory authorities may rebut the controller's analysis and demand clear evidence, no EU establishment means dealing with every local authority, and Recital 36 putting the processor under the controller's lead authority all confirmed.

Attribution settled: the paper is headed 'ARTICLE 29 DATA PROTECTION WORKING PARTY' and titled 'WORKING PARTY 29 POSITION PAPER', and speaks throughout as 'The WP29', so attributing it to WP29 is right; 19 April 2018 predates the Working Party's 25 May 2018 dissolution. Text confirms the three conditions are alternative, 'the occurrence of any one of them alone triggers the obligation', that records are needed 'only ... for the types of processing mentioned by Article 30(5)', and the employee-data example.
